items.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000
items.q: It’s like how can you duplicate Trane? How can you duplicate Bird or Sweets or Prez or Diz?

ctx.x: Too clean, yeah. Too much in the amplification. If you start making the bass too loud it affects the way the music was conceived I think.

It’s like how can you duplicate Trane? How can you duplicate Bird or Sweets or Prez or Diz? You know it’s just like these so-called radio stations. They call themselves jazz stations. Now I purposely don’t listen to them, but I listened to them all last week, right? Because I was home. And the whole length of time I was listening to them, the whole week, I think they played one Charlie Parker record, and one Dizzy Gillespie record. A whole week. Never Chico Hamilton.
Yeah, I was going to say, did you get in there.

items.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: we were sitting on the bandstand and we’re talking man, and Trane says, Cheeks, I’ve played myself into a box

ctx.x: Let me since I brought up John Coltrane, you know, we inevitably have to talk about Elvin Jones because, you know, you talk about these very crucial periods in your development.

You know, John told me -- we were sitting on the bandstand at the ID Club in LA. You know, John Coltrane, John c, the original godfather, and it was on a Sunday afternoon, man, a matinee. I went to see John. I went to see Trane rather and we were sitting on the bandstand and we’re talking man, and Trane says, Cheeks, I’ve played myself into a box. And I asked him, I said what do you mean? He says well, there’s just so many places I can play. He says whereas you play all over. You play in Chicago, you play the…
Do you remember about what year this was for Trane, for you I guess I should say, but I’m just trying to think about -­
